content: 1. An algorithm should be developed and implemented in the screening area to ensure systematic and effective identification of suspected cases. 2. Hand hygiene stations must be made available in the screening area to promote infection control practices. 3. Alcohol-based hand rub (ABHR) or soap and water should ideally be used for hand hygiene. Soap and water are specifically recommended for visibly soiled hands. 4. A 0.5% chlorine solution should be made available for handwashing purposes. 5. Posters illustrating proper hand hygiene techniques should be displayed prominently to guide healthcare workers and visitors. 6. Dedicated cleaning and disinfection supplies should be provided to maintain a sterile environment. 7. Waste bins, including those for sharps disposal, should be available to ensure proper waste management. 8. A referral system must be established to manage individuals who meet the suspect case definition. This system should include mechanisms for validation, safe transport, and temporary isolation. 9. Rapid and early identification of suspected cases of Ebola Virus Disease (EVD) or Marburg Virus Disease (MVD) is critical for source control, such as isolating cases, and for preventing disease transmission. 10. During outbreaks of Ebola or Marburg disease, all individuals (patients, visitors, and healthcare workers) in areas where these viruses are circulating should be screened using a no-touch technique at the first point of contact with any healthcare facility. This enables early recognition of suspected cases and rapid implementation of source control measures. 11. Infection prevention and control (IPC) guidelines emphasize the importance of rapid identification and implementation of control measures, such as isolating suspected or confirmed cases, to prevent transmission. 12. Screening and triage processes may be conducted in the same physical space by the same person in smaller facilities, while in larger facilities, these processes are often performed separately by different personnel. 13. Every healthcare facility in areas with circulating Ebola or Marburg viruses should have a dedicated, well-equipped triage area. This area should include: At least 1 meter of spacing between beds or assessment spaces. Adequate space for donning and doffing personal protective equipment (PPE), including space for a buddy to assist during PPE removal. Hand hygiene stations. Sufficient patient care equipment to allow cleaning and disinfection between uses. Waste bins with lids and sharps containers. 14. Triage is an established process for ensuring quality care during outbreaks and for patients suspected of having symptoms of pathogens of concern, such as Ebola or Marburg viruses. It ensures safe and essential care delivery. 15. All patients, including those presenting for surgery, obstetrics, or other invasive procedures, who are suspected of having Ebola or Marburg disease, should be triaged to assess the severity of their illness and identify those requiring immediate care. 16. Personal protective equipment (PPE) for healthcare workers should meet the preferred product characteristics outlined by the World Health Organization (WHO). For example: Gowns and coveralls should meet fluid-resistance standards to protect against blood and body fluids. If gowns or coveralls lack high fluid resistance at the front, an apron should be added. Fluid-resistant medical or surgical masks with a structured design that does not collapse against the mouth are preferred. 17. Medical masks that collapse when wet may allow fluid permeation. Dome-shaped, cup-shaped, duckbill-shaped, or flat-paneled respirators are often used as alternatives. 18. Healthcare workers conducting screening activities should maintain a distance of at least 1 meter and follow a no-touch policy. PPE is not required if these conditions are met. 19. In situations where maintaining a 1-meter distance or a no-touch policy is not possible, healthcare workers should conduct a risk assessment to determine the need for PPE. This may include a medical mask, eye protection, a gown, and gloves if contact with body fluids is anticipated. 20. Hand hygiene should be performed according to WHO’s 5 Moments for Hand Hygiene guidelines. 21. Excessive use of PPE can paradoxically increase the risk of infection. Proper training on screening procedures and appropriate PPE use is essential. 22. Screening areas should be designed to maintain a 1-meter distance between the screener and the individual being screened. Physical barriers, such as tables or plexiglass, can help ensure this distance. 23. Non-contact thermometers should be used to facilitate no-touch screening techniques. 24. Masks should be replaced when wet. If off-the-face designs are unavailable, respirators may be considered. 25. Gowns or coveralls should be fluid-resistant. If not, an apron should be added for additional protection. 26. Medical scrubs are considered regular on-duty wear and are not classified as PPE. Scrubs should be tightly woven, minimize linting, and can be reusable or single-use. Tops should be short-sleeved, and trousers should have a drawstring waist closure. 27. Scrubs worn when caring for suspected or confirmed Ebola or Marburg patients should be removed when soiled or at the end of the shift and laundered at the healthcare facility. They should not be taken home for laundering. 28. Healthcare workers should wear closed-toe shoes, such as slip-ons without shoelaces, that fully cover the dorsum of the foot and ankle. Rubber boots are preferred in settings where care is provided to suspected or confirmed cases, as they offer additional protection against sharps injuries and are easier to decontaminate. 29. Waterproof rubber boots should be knee-high to provide sufficient coverage and should have non-slip PVC soles. Light-colored boots are preferred for better detection of contamination. 30. During screening activities, gloves or other PPE are not required if a 1-meter distance and no-touch policy can be maintained. However, if these conditions cannot be met, appropriate PPE, such as eye protection and medical masks, should be used. 31. The use of non-contact thermometers and physical barriers, such as plexiglass, is recommended to maintain a safe distance during screening. 32. The WHO emphasizes that PPE is not required during screening activities in healthcare settings if a 1-meter distance and no-touch approach are strictly followed. However, in cases where these measures cannot be guaranteed, appropriate PPE should be used based on risk assessment.
